scenario: AITA for no longer cooking for my roommate because he dumps condiments on everything? | Because I love cooking and (at the risk of sounding arrogant) I'm pretty good at it, I've always volunteered to be in charge of dinner when dividing up chores with roommates. I'm **not** saying my food is perfect. There are a lot of things I'm trying to improve on. But I learned to cook from two professional chefs, I don't have a lot of typical issues like under-seasoning or over-cooking food, and even when I'm living with other people that are also good at cooking I'm usually asked to prepare food 3+ nights a week. Even if I'm not incredible, I at least know what I'm doing. Since this comes up later: we have a shared food budget for staples/basic ingredients (pasta, broth, canned vegetables, flour, sugar, spices, etc). Half the time we'll split the cost of meat and fresh ingredients, half the time I pay for them myself and and accept booze, snacks (another roommate is a phenomenal baker), chores, or favors as payment. The problem is, one of my newer roommates puts condiments on everything he eats. I'm not just talking about things like hamburgers, chicken wings, mac and cheese, or anything else that normally gets condiments. I've seen him put ketchup, mayo, hot sauce, A1, or barbeque sauce on chili, steak, alfredo, fried rice, curry, pizza, red sauce, gumbo, ribs that are already covered in BBQ sauce... you get the idea. And that would be fine, I guess, but he A) does it without even trying the food first and B) completely smothers the food with them. I've tried to talk to him about this. I offered to make his favorite meals, but even stuff he says he likes prepared the way he says he likes it gets the same treatment. I've asked him to at least try the food first but he refuses. I've explained that it bothers me when I put effort into a meal and he treats it the same way he treats fast food and microwave dinners, but he said it was still being eaten so it didn't matter. I finally got frustrated and told him not to give me anything for fresh ingredients anymore because I was done cooking for him. He's been complaining to my other two roommates because his monthly expenses have gone way up (he doesn't cook at all, so he either eats out or buys prepackage meals) and saying that I'm being petty and over dramatic. My baking roommate says she agrees with my decision and the other roommate doesn't care, he just wants mealtimes to be less dramatic. AITA? I think I did plenty to meet him halfway.

Sewing or altering clothes may also add to the expense. 2. **Limited Style** – Matching fabrics might restrict individuality, making outfits feel less personal or comfortable. 3. **Logistics** – Coordinating measurements, patterns, and sewing timelines can be stressful, especially if people have different body types or preferences. 4. **Wearability** – If the fabric is formal (e.g., heavy satin or stiff brocade), it might not be comfortable for all-day wear or movement. 5. **Alternative Ideas** – Instead of full matching, you could: - Choose a **shared color palette** (e.g., everyone wears a shade of blue or gold). - Opt for **similar silhouettes** (e.g., all dresses with the same neckline or pants with matching details). - Use **accessories** (e.g., coordinated scarves, shoes, or jewelry) for a subtle touch. ### **Questions to Ask Yourself:** - **Is this a family expectation or tradition?** If it’s deeply meaningful, it might be worth it. - **How much flexibility do you have in styling?** Could you mix fabrics or patterns in a way that feels intentional? - **What’s the budget?** Could you compromise (e.g., matching shoes or bags instead of full outfits)? - **How do you feel about uniformity vs. individuality?** Would you prefer to stand out or blend in? ### **Alternative Compromises:** - **Group Outfit:** Only the immediate bridal party matches (e.g., bridesmaids + groomsmen in coordinated pieces). - **Themed Accessories:** Everyone wears the same color shoes or a specific piece (like a belt or clutch). - **Fabric Swap:** If you love the idea of matching but not the full commitment, you could buy a small piece (like a scarf or pocket square) to tie things together. prediction.raw: **Answer: 1 (You did the right thing, but with room for nuance).** ### **Why?** 1. **You’ve Already Given Him Multiple Chances** - You offered to cook his favorite meals, explained your feelings, and even tried to accommodate his preferences. That’s fair. But when someone repeatedly disregards basic respect for your effort—especially after clear communication—it’s reasonable to set boundaries. 2. **His Behavior Is Unreasonable** - Dumping condiments on *everything* (even dishes that don’t traditionally need them) isn’t just picky—it’s disrespectful. Food is meant to be enjoyed, not ruined by overpowering sauces. His refusal to even *try* the food first (a basic courtesy) shows a lack of consideration. - His argument that "it’s still being eaten" ignores the fact that you’re putting effort into meals, and his actions make them feel like fast food—undermining the value of your cooking. 3. **You’re Not Being Petty—You’re Protecting Your Labor** - You’ve been the primary cook for years, and your skills are recognized by others. Withholding payment for fresh ingredients isn’t about punishment—it’s about enforcing a basic expectation: *If you don’t respect the food, you don’t get to benefit from it without contributing.* - His complaint about "expenses" is hypocritical—if he’s not cooking, he should either: - **Eat what’s made** (even if he doesn’t like it). - **Cook for himself** (like a responsible adult). - **Pay for his own meals** (if he’s unwilling to participate). 4. **Your Roommates’ Reactions Matter** - Your baking roommate agrees with you—that’s a strong sign you’re on the right track. - The neutral roommate’s indifference isn’t a vote against you; it just means he doesn’t care either way (which is fine—this isn’t his problem). ### **Where There’s Room for Growth (But Not Apologies)** - **Clarify the Boundaries Upfront** - Next time, you could say: > *"I’m happy to cook for everyone, but if you’re going to ruin the food with condiments, I expect you to either eat it as-is or not take any ingredients from me. If you don’t like it, cook your own meal."* - This removes ambiguity and makes it clear that his behavior has consequences. - **Document the Agreement** - Since you have a shared budget, you could write down: > *"If you take fresh ingredients from the shared budget, you agree to eat the resulting meals without altering them in a way that ruins them (e.g., drowning in condiments)."* - This protects you legally and emotionally if he complains further. - **Lead by Example** - If he’s struggling with food preferences, you could occasionally offer to cook *his* version of a dish (e.g., "I’ll make you a burger with ketchup if you promise not to put it on steak"). But don’t keep doing this indefinitely—it’s not your job to cater to someone who refuses basic respect. ### **Final Verdict** You didn’t overreact. His behavior was unreasonable, and your decision was fair, necessary, and even kind (you gave him multiple chances). If he can’t respect the effort, he shouldn’t expect to benefit from it without reciprocity. **Bonus Thought:** If this keeps happening, consider whether this is a roommate who values shared living—or just shared resources. Sometimes, people who don’t contribute to the *emotional* side of living together (like respecting others’ efforts) aren’t worth the hassle.
